variants.title: Walk the evidence path
variants.context: A multimodal request walks five stages: validate each source at the boundary, encode by modality, align the evidence, fuse it for the task, then ground and govern the answer. Alignment and fallback are first-class stages, not cleanup after inference.
variants.prompt: A support ticket arrives with a photo of a damaged part. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Fuse the aligned evidence at the boundary chosen for this task.
Check media type, size, duration, timestamp, integrity, consent, and trust zone before decoding.
Encode text and image with their own transforms, preserving preprocessing versions and coordinates.
Match the photo to the ticket entity and time window, exposing any missing relationship.
Return evidence references, uncertainty, modality state, model version, and a bounded product action.

variants.hint: One stage decides whether the expensive stages should run at all.
variants.explanation: Validation happens before decoding so malformed or stale evidence never reaches the model, and governance happens after fusion so the action stays bounded by what the evidence supports.

variants.title: Walk the evidence path
variants.context: A multimodal request walks five stages: validate each source at the boundary, encode by modality, align the evidence, fuse it for the task, then ground and govern the answer. Alignment and fallback are first-class stages, not cleanup after inference.
variants.prompt: A meeting recording is paired with a slide deck that may be older than the talk. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Map each slide to the transcript window it belongs to and expose the pairs that do not match.
Return the summary with references, the stale-pair state, and the action the system took.
Encode audio and slide images separately, keeping timestamps and preprocessing versions.
Fuse only the evidence whose alignment was established for the summary task.
Validate both files for media type, duration, integrity, and capture time.

variants.hint: Paired files are not the same thing as aligned files.
variants.explanation: Alignment is an explicit stage with its own failure output, because two sources can be individually valid and still describe different moments.

variants.title: Walk the evidence path
variants.context: A multimodal request walks five stages: validate each source at the boundary, encode by modality, align the evidence, fuse it for the task, then ground and govern the answer. Alignment and fallback are first-class stages, not cleanup after inference.
variants.prompt: An uploaded screenshot contains text that reads like an instruction to the assistant. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Align the extracted text with the request entity and time window it claims to describe.
Validate the upload's media type, size, digest, and trust zone before any decoding.
Fuse the evidence for the task while application authority stays with the request, not the media.
Return the answer with evidence references, the safety decision, and the modality state.
Encode the image and extract its text as content from an untrusted zone.

variants.hint: Ask which stage assigns the trust zone that later stages rely on.
variants.explanation: Extracted text is evidence, never instruction, so the trust zone assigned at validation is what keeps embedded content from acquiring system or tool authority.

variants.title: Release the system, not the checkpoint
variants.context: A multimodal release ships a system, not a checkpoint: freeze the input contract, measure complete and degraded slices, shadow the full path, then canary with bounded product authority while the previous compatible path stays loadable.
variants.prompt: A new vision-language model is ready for a document assistant. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Canary with limited traffic and bounded product actions while the previous compatible path stays loadable.
Compare fused and unimodal behavior, then inject missing, stale, corrupted, conflicting, and untrusted inputs.
Shadow the full path to capture decode failures, modality availability, token volume, alignment lag, and latency.
Version media limits, preprocessing, alignment rules, required modalities, trust zones, and fallback ownership.

variants.hint: Degraded slices only mean something once the contract they violate is written down.
variants.explanation: The input contract is frozen first because every later measurement, shadow trace, and rollback depends on knowing which evidence was required.

variants.title: Release the system, not the checkpoint
variants.context: A multimodal release ships a system, not a checkpoint: freeze the input contract, measure complete and degraded slices, shadow the full path, then canary with bounded product authority while the previous compatible path stays loadable.
variants.prompt: Only the image preprocessing changes: higher resolution and a new crop rule, with the same weights. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Canary with the previous preprocessing kept loadable for rollback.
Re-measure complete and degraded slices, because a preprocessing change can move the decision on its own.
Version the new media limits and crop rule as a change to the input contract.
Shadow the path to see the new token volume, decode failure rate, and end-to-end latency.

variants.hint: A checkpoint rollback cannot undo a change that lives outside the checkpoint.
variants.explanation: Preprocessing, token budgets, and alignment metadata are part of the released contract, so changing one of them requires the same evidence and rollback path as new weights.

variants.title: Release the system, not the checkpoint
variants.context: A multimodal release ships a system, not a checkpoint: freeze the input contract, measure complete and degraded slices, shadow the full path, then canary with bounded product authority while the previous compatible path stays loadable.
variants.prompt: An audio channel is being added to a system that already uses text and images. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Canary with bounded authority while the text and image path remains the fallback.
Measure the fused path against the unimodal baselines so the new source's contribution is visible.
Extend the input contract with the audio limits, alignment rule, trust zone, and fallback owner.
Shadow the full path for decode failures, alignment lag, audio duration, and queue time.

variants.hint: Ask what proves the new modality is being used at all.
variants.explanation: A new modality is justified by its measured contribution against unimodal baselines, since adding a source can leave the model quietly ignoring the expensive one.

variants.title: Count what the modalities cost
variants.context: Multimodal cost is driven by the shape of the media. Resolution, frame rate, and duration set the visual token volume, language evidence adds its own tokens, and dense cross-attention compares every visual token with every language token.
variants.prompt: A page image is encoded as 1,200 visual tokens, and the prompt plus transcript come to 800 language tokens. How many cross-modal token pairs does dense cross-attention compare?
variants.hint: Dense means every token on one side meets every token on the other.
variants.explanation: Dense cross-attention compares 1,200 visual tokens with 800 language tokens, which is 960,000 pairs.

mistakes.feedback: 2,000 adds the two sequences, which is the token count, not the interaction count.
1,440,000 squares the visual tokens, which is visual self-attention rather than cross-modal work.

variants.title: Count what the modalities cost
variants.context: Multimodal cost is driven by the shape of the media. Resolution, frame rate, and duration set the visual token volume, language evidence adds its own tokens, and dense cross-attention compares every visual token with every language token.
variants.prompt: A product change doubles the visual tokens and triples the language tokens for the same request. By what factor does the dense cross-modal pair work grow?
variants.hint: The pair count is a product of the two lengths, so ask what happens to a product.
variants.explanation: Cross-modal pair work is visual tokens times language tokens, so doubling one and tripling the other multiplies the work by 6.

mistakes.feedback: 5 adds the two growth factors instead of multiplying them.
3 counts only the language growth and ignores the extra visual tokens it now attends to.

variants.title: Count what the modalities cost
variants.context: Multimodal cost is driven by the shape of the media. Resolution, frame rate, and duration set the visual token volume, language evidence adds its own tokens, and dense cross-attention compares every visual token with every language token.
variants.prompt: A 30 second clip is sampled at 2 frames per second and each frame becomes 256 visual tokens. How many visual tokens does the request carry?
variants.hint: Duration and frame rate decide how many frames exist before tokens are counted.
variants.explanation: 30 seconds at 2 frames per second is 60 frames, and 60 frames at 256 tokens each is 15,360 visual tokens.

mistakes.feedback: 7,680 uses 30 frames, which is one frame per second rather than the sampled 2.
512 multiplies the frame rate by the tokens per frame and never uses the clip duration.

variants.title: Choose the fusion boundary
variants.context: Fusion is the point where modalities begin to influence one decision. A shared-space dual encoder gives precomputable similarity, token-level cross-attention gives fine grounding at a cost that grows with both sequences, and late fusion with a gate keeps modality paths independent so the system can route or abstain.
variants.prompt: An assistant must answer questions about a specific value inside a chart image and point at the region it used. Which boundary fits?
options: A shared-space dual encoder, so image and question vectors can be compared directly.
Token-level cross-attention, so language tokens can select the visual evidence they need.
Late fusion with a gate, so each modality keeps its own independent prediction.
optionFeedback: A shared space produces similarity between whole items, not token-level grounding inside one image.
Correct: fine grounding needs one modality's tokens to attend to specific regions of the other.
Independent paths never represent the interaction, so the gate has nothing fine-grained to combine.
variants.hint: Ask what the answer must point at, not just what it must be about.
variants.explanation: The boundary follows the task: grounded, region-level answers need token interaction, which is exactly the cost that grows with both sequence lengths.

variants.title: Choose the fusion boundary
variants.context: Fusion is the point where modalities begin to influence one decision. A shared-space dual encoder gives precomputable similarity, token-level cross-attention gives fine grounding at a cost that grows with both sequences, and late fusion with a gate keeps modality paths independent so the system can route or abstain.
variants.prompt: A safety-sensitive machine uses a camera and motion telemetry, and either source can fail on its own. Which boundary fits?
options: One shared embedding space that places camera and telemetry evidence together.
Late fusion with a gate that can route or abstain when one source is unavailable.
Token-level cross-attention across the video frames and the telemetry stream.
optionFeedback: A shared space gives similarity, not the availability-aware routing a safety system needs.
Correct: independent paths keep each source monitorable and let the gate abstain when the contract is unmet.
Dense interaction couples the paths, so a failed camera degrades the whole prediction in ways that are hard to observe.
variants.hint: Which design still has something meaningful to say when one sensor drops out?
variants.explanation: Safety-sensitive systems favor explicit independent paths and a gate, because availability-aware routing and per-modality monitoring matter more than fine interaction.

variants.title: Choose the fusion boundary
variants.context: Fusion is the point where modalities begin to influence one decision. A shared-space dual encoder gives precomputable similarity, token-level cross-attention gives fine grounding at a cost that grows with both sequences, and late fusion with a gate keeps modality paths independent so the system can route or abstain.
variants.prompt: A required image fails to decode at request time and the task expects it. What should the system do?
options: Fill the missing image with an average embedding so a prediction is still returned.
Generate a caption from the text and use it in place of the visual evidence.
Narrow the task or abstain, and label any substitution as its own operating mode.
optionFeedback: An average embedding preserves the tensor shape while quietly presenting absent evidence as ordinary input.
A caption derived from the other modality adds no independent evidence and can repeat its errors.
Correct: missing required evidence changes the operating mode, and that mode is labeled and evaluated separately.
variants.hint: Ask whether the substitute carries information the missing source would have carried.
variants.explanation: Preserving an input shape is not restoring evidence, so substitutions become named operating modes with their own measured consequences.

variants.title: Record the modality contract
variants.context: A modality is more than a tensor. The contract records what it is, why it belongs to this event, whether it is required, how far it may be trusted, and which product actions it can support at all.
variants.prompt: Match each property of the modality contract to what it records.

pairs.label: Representation
pairs.detail: Media type, shape, sample rate, resolution, encoding, preprocessing version, and tokenization.

pairs.label: Alignment key
pairs.detail: The request ID, timestamp, entity, region, or transform explaining why sources share one event.

pairs.label: Availability
pairs.detail: Whether the source is required, optional, delayed, retryable, reconstructable, or permanently absent.

pairs.label: Trust and rights
pairs.detail: Origin, consent, retention, privacy class, and whether extracted content may influence instructions.

pairs.label: Authority
pairs.detail: Which product actions this source supports alone, only in combination, or never.

variants.hint: Two of these describe the bytes; the rest describe what the bytes are allowed to do.
variants.explanation: The five properties together are what make a prediction traceable to the evidence that was required, the evidence that arrived, and the fallback that owned the decision.

variants.title: Record the modality contract
variants.context: A modality is more than a tensor. The contract records what it is, why it belongs to this event, whether it is required, how far it may be trusted, and which product actions it can support at all.
variants.prompt: Match each way two modalities can relate to what it means for the system.

pairs.label: Complementary evidence
pairs.detail: The sources describe different aspects of one event, such as intent in text and location in an image.

pairs.label: Redundant evidence
pairs.detail: Two sources observe the same property, so agreement raises confidence and disagreement becomes a visible state.

pairs.label: Correlated noise
pairs.detail: Two sources repeat the same bias, timestamp error, or upstream label, so they are not independent evidence.

variants.hint: Ask whether a second source could ever contradict the first.
variants.explanation: Adding a modality only helps when it carries evidence the others do not, which is why disagreement and shared failure are designed for rather than assumed away.

variants.title: Record the modality contract
variants.context: A modality is more than a tensor. The contract records what it is, why it belongs to this event, whether it is required, how far it may be trusted, and which product actions it can support at all.
variants.prompt: Match each evaluation condition to what it exposes about the system.

pairs.label: Unimodal baselines
pairs.detail: Whether one path dominates and how much the expensive modality actually contributes.

pairs.label: Missing modality
pairs.detail: How the system behaves when a required or optional source never arrives.

pairs.label: Corrupted modality
pairs.detail: Whether realistic blur, noise, or truncation degrades quality gracefully or silently.

pairs.label: Stale or misaligned modality
pairs.detail: Whether shifted timestamps, wrong entities, or bad transforms are detected instead of fused.

pairs.label: Untrusted content
pairs.detail: Whether instructions embedded in media can change the application's authority.

variants.hint: Each row breaks the happy path in one specific way.
variants.explanation: One aggregate benchmark cannot show which modality was used or how the system behaves when production inputs violate the contract, so each condition is measured on its own.
